title: Impact of Future Methane Emission Trajectories on Atmospheric Composition and Climate in a Future Hydrogen Economy
content:
Abstract

Hydrogen (H2 ${\mathrm{H}}_{2}$) is projected to have an increasingly important role in a future low-carbon economy. In a future H2 ${\mathrm{H}}_{2}$ economy, H2 ${\mathrm{H}}_{2}$ emissions could increase across the supply chain. When H2 ${\mathrm{H}}_{2}$, a radiatively inert gas, is emitted, it undergoes similar chemical reactions to methane (CH4 ${\mathrm{H}}_{4}$) in the atmosphere, leading to detrimental climate as well as air quality effects. Here, we study the interactions between hypothetical future increases in H2 ${\mathrm{H}}_{2}$ emissions and possible future CH4 ${\mathrm{H}}_{4}$ emission trajectories, utilizing the GFDL AM4.1 atmospheric chemistry-climate model (CCM) driven by H2 ${\mathrm{H}}_{2}$ and CH4 ${\mathrm{H}}_{4}$ emissions to more fully simulate their chemical feedbacks. Due to their chemical coupling, the effects of H2 ${\mathrm{H}}_{2}$ on atmospheric composition are dependent on background CH4 ${\mathrm{H}}_{4}$ emission levels. However, despite this dependency, the climate impact of H2 ${\mathrm{H}}_{2}$ remains largely independent of background CH4 ${\mathrm{H}}_{4}$ emission levels, because of offsetting changes in the forcing from radiatively active gases as well as model rapid adjustments. Next, we find that an ambitious 45% anthropogenic CH4 ${\mathrm{H}}_{4}$ emission reduction not only delivers greater surface cooling than the surface warming caused from a hypothetical high-end 480% H2 ${\mathrm{H}}_{2}$ emission increase, but also effectively counteracts the atmospheric composition impacts from the increase in H2 ${\mathrm{H}}_{2}$ emissions as well. Increased H2 ${\mathrm{H}}_{2}$ adoption in an H2 ${\mathrm{H}}_{2}$ economy, replacing fossil fuels, could contribute to reductions in other short-lived climate forcer emissions, such as ozone precursors and aerosols. When these additional reductions are considered, CH4 ${\mathrm{H}}_{4}$ mitigation is increasingly important so as to maximize the climate and air quality benefits of an H2 ${\mathrm{H}}_{2}$ economy.
